title: ‘Maggie Thatcher, can you hear me?’ The story behind the iconic Norway v England commentary - The Guardian
content: Bjørge Lillelien’s famous rant after 1981 clash stemmed from Norwegian obsession with English football What do Lord Nelson, Lord Beaverbrook, Sir Winston Churchill, Sir Anthony Eden, Clement Attlee, Henry Cooper and Lady Diana have in common? On 9 September 1981 they were all beaten by Norway. At least that is according to the iconic Norwegian radio commentator Bjørge Lillelien. His triumphant, giddy and slightly unhinged rant after Norway beat England 2-1 in a World Cup qualifier has gone down in Norwegian folklore. It has also attained something of a cult status abroad, with the Observer declaring it in 2002 the greatest bit of commentary ever. “We have beaten England! England, the birthplace of giants!” Lillelien enthused, before listing some of said giants. Henry Cooper may seem an odd man out among the various statesmen and Lady Di, but then Lillelien was a notable boxing aficionado. “Maggie Thatcher, can you hear me? I have a message for you, in the middle of your election campaign. I have a message for you … As they say in the boxing bars around Madison Square Garden in New York: your boys took a hell of a beating! Your boys took a hell of a beating!” For those last two sentences Lillelien switched to English, just in case Maggie Thatcher could in fact hear him. At the time, Lillelien’s elation may have seemed a little excessive to some English observers. Norway were, after all, not the only team that beat England in 1981. Earlier that year they had lost to Switzerland, Scotland, Spain and Brazil, as well as drawn against Wales and Romania. The year before they had lost to Romania, Italy and Wales. They were hardly an unstoppable force. But in 1981 England had a special place in Norwegian footballing hearts that no poor run of form could diminish. Since November 1969 the Norwegian public broadcaster NRK had been showing live matches from the English first division during the winter, when Norwegian football was on a weather-enforced hiatus. With Norway having one television channel at the time, that meant every person who wanted to watch TV on a Saturday afternoon during those months would be watching English football. And the games enthralled the nation. “We would learn on Wednesday what game was going to be shown on NRK at the weekend, and there was a lot of excitement around that,” says Øyvind Alsaker, who will be commentating on Saturday’s World Cup quarter-final against England for the Norwegian broadcaster TV2. “Would your team be shown?” Alsaker, born in 1969, was part of the first generation that grew up with these televised games. “You would run outside and pretend to be Keegan and Toshack and all of these heroes,” he says. But it wasn’t always the big teams shown. On 14 January 1978, for instance, NRK somehow ended up showing Mansfield taking on Southampton in the second division – which, with all due respect to the Stags, must have seemed slightly baffling to the Norwegians. But this did lead to people in Norway forming emotional attachments to unlikely clubs. Gabriel Høyland, Erling Haaland’s great uncle who earned 23 caps for Norway, is a committed Burnley supporter. Kasper Wikestad, who commentated on Norway’s win against Brazil for NRK this week, is a Norwich fan. He was one of many Norwegians who grew up with England as his footballing nirvana. “It was the sound, the smell, the stars; it was the atmosphere, it was the chants from the stands,” he says. “It was our promised land. It felt so close, but at the same time so far away.” If England were going through a tough spell in 1981, Norway were just not very good. “It was a Norwegian national team that hadn’t been to a tournament in any kind of way since the 1938 Olympics,” Wikestad says. “England were our idols and our reference point. For Norwegians at that time, England and English football was like a dream. How good England were, how big the stars were, everything to do with England was huge. The idea that we could beat England at football in a qualifying match, it was a totally unrealistic dream.” Lillelien had always been something of an entertainer. “He was a man who made boring games fun,” Alsaker says. “We would turn on the sound from the radio, and watch the game on with the TV on mute.” With Norway taking a 2-1 lead and holding on for a historic win against England, Lillelien was already fraying at the edges. As Phil Neal hacked down the local hero Tom Lund from behind Lillelien erupted, calling Neal “a pig”. “The thug Phil Neal kicks Tommy from behind! Phil ‘pig’ Neal! Start retaliating! The English have thugs both in the stands and on the pitch!” Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football As the seconds ticked away into added time, Lillelien felt the Polish referee, Jerzy Kacprzak, was too slow to blow the final whistle. “The referee keeps adding and adding and adding, he is on track for an English citizenship!” But just as this aspersion was cast, Kacprzak blew and Lillelien erupted again. “Norway have beaten England 2-1 at football! We are the best in the world!” And you know the rest. Today, Norwegians are still obsessed with English football. Norwegian kids grow up dreaming of playing in England, more so than at Barcelona or Real Madrid or anywhere else. “We now have three generations of Norwegians who have received English football intravenously,” Alsaker says. On Saturday it will be his job to convey the emotion of the occasion back to the Norwegian public. “It feels unreal. When I look at what I’ve experienced with the Norwegian national team over the last 25 years, it feels unreal that this is happening. I was thinking that reaching the round of 16 was just fantastic. And now we are playing for being one of the top four teams at a World Cup. It’s wild. It is a task I approach with great humility and a feeling of responsibility. So many Norwegians will be following this, I hope I will succeed in doing a good job. “Norway-England, of all things. A week ago, we thought that it couldn’t get bigger than Norway-Brazil, but there you go.” For Norwegians, no opponent we face on a football pitch could ever mean more than England.

title: Sony's RX10 V Superzoom Finally Arrives With A New Design And 4K 120p Video - Engadget
content: Sony has finally unveiled the RX10 V, a superzoom compact camera that comes with a 24-600mm optical zoom lens and 20.1-megapixel 1-inch sensor. The design has been overhauled compared to the nine-year-old RX10 IV for a more modern look and adds faster speeds, an updated autofocus system and far better video specs. The catch is the $2,300 price, which makes this one of the most expensive compact cameras on the market. As before, the RX10 V offers tourists, street shooters and others incredible reach thanks to the 9.1-210mm (24-600mm equivalent) f2.4-4.0 lens. The 20.1MP 1-inch stacked sensor appears unchanged and should deliver good-quality images, even in low light, with minimal rolling shutter distortion. It's disappointing that Sony didn't upgrade the resolution, though, especially considering the camera's price. The new model also lacks the RX10 IV's built-in flash. The new model does have a new processor that improved burst speeds, though. It can now shoot at 30 fps with no blackout in electronic shutter mode, a nice upgrade over the previous model's 24 fps shooting speeds. Sony also carried over a feature from its latest mirrorless cameras called "continuous shooting speed boost" that lets you instantly jump to the maximum burst speed to capture decisive moments. Autofocus also got a big AI makeover to match the new A7 V. Rather than just humans and animals as before, it can detect the face, eye, head and body of humans, birds and animals, along with vehicles (cars, trains and airplanes) and insects (head and whole body). Thanks to a separate deep AI processor, it will keep tracking subjects even if they turn away, look down or move in an erratic fashion. AF and AE speed has also doubled to 60 fps for continuous tracking, and it now offers 575 AF points compared to 315 before, along with 70 percent sensor coverage. Video gets perhaps the biggest upgrade, with 4K 60 fps 10-bit video (All-Intra, XAVC S, and XAVC HS formats) that uses the entire sensor width with no pixel binning for extra sharpness. That can be boosted to 4K 120 fps for super slow mo, at the cost of a slight crop, or 1080p at 240 fps. It also supports Sony's S-Log3 for improved dynamic range and lets you import up to 16 LUTs to preview different "looks" ahead of time. Sony also improved the built-in stabilization so that it smooths video even when you're walking with it. The design was completely revamped compared RX10 IV's bulbous, stodgy look. It's now sleeker and more squared off to match the A7 V's aesthetic and has a much larger grip. It comes with a full complement of manual controls including a joystick, three control dials, a control wheel and a new dual top dial (with a photo, video and S&Q selector), plus an AF-ON button for pro autofocus control. Both the electronic viewfinder (EVF) and rear display get resolution upgrades to 3.69 million dots (up from 2.4 million dots) and 1.62 million dots respectively. However, the rear display only tilts and doesn't flip out, so it's not great for vlogging or selfies. Again, that's a rather inexcusable omission considering the camera's price. Other features include a single UHS-II SD card slot, full-sized NP-FZ100 battery that delivers up to 630 shots on a charge, a micro HDMI port 3.5mm mic and headphone ports and a new high-speed USB-C port for charging and transfers. The RX10 V now supports live streaming at up to 4K 30 fps as well. Now for the bad news if you're interested in this new model. The RX10 V just went on pre-order for $2,300 (with shipping in August), a relative fortune for a 1-inch compact camera. If that price is in your wheelhouse, though, it does offer incredible zoom reach, shooting speeds and video capabilities.

title: Sony RX10 V First Look: One Camera, Every Shot - Fstoppers
content: I had the good fortune of spending some time with Sony's new RX10 V, and I shot the entire range of my life with it. A World Cup match here in Seattle one weekend, then a family outing to the Ballard Locks the next. The promise of the Sony RX10 V is a simple one: leave with one camera, come home with every photo. Let's take a look at why, for me, that promise mostly holds up. Building on the RX10 IV, this update includes the latest BIONZ XR processing engine, a dedicated AI processing unit, Real-time Recognition AF, and blackout-free 30 fps shooting. That is a meaningful generational leap for Sony's most versatile all-in-one bridge camera. The headline here is still that ZEISS Vario-Sonnar T* zoom. A 24-600mm equivalent range with a bright f/2.4-4.0 aperture is the kind of reach that normally equates to carrying a bag full of glass, but on the RX10 V, all of those focal lengths live in a single lens with Optical SteadyShot built in. At the Ballard Locks, I framed a wide shot of some sculptures at 24mm, then pushed all the way to 600mm to fill the frame, all in one motion. For me, that kind of flexibility and convenience is the entire reason this camera exists. What surprised me the most was the close-focusing. At the wide end it focuses down to roughly 3 cm, so the same body that reaches across the locks for a diving seagull can double as a macro camera for frame-filling detail. Wide angle, super-telephoto, and macro in one grab is a genuinely rare combination. This is where the new processing of the RX10 V really shows. The BIONZ XR engine and dedicated AI chip drive Real-time Recognition AF across an impressive spread of subjects: human, animal, bird, insect, and several vehicle types, with roughly 575 phase-detection points covering about 70% of the frame. At the locks, I put the bird recognition on seagulls diving over the water, and it latched onto them against a busy, moving background easily. When action peaks, the RX10 V fires at up to 30 fps completely blackout-free, with up to 60 AF/AE calculations per second. The blackout-free electronic viewfinder is critical for me when I'm tracking fast action, because I never lose sight of my subject mid-burst. The RX10 V also has a popular feature from Sony's flagship cameras like the a1 II and a9 III. Continuous Shooting Speed Boost is available, and can be assigned to a custom button to jump to your maximum frame rate only at the critical moment, so you're not wading through thousands of frames after your shoot. The video side of the Sony RX10 V is just as serious as its stills features, and pretty impressive for an all-in-one bridge camera: What stuck with me after two weeks of shooting with the Sony RX10 V wasn't any single spec; it was how little I thought about managing a bunch of gear. One battery comfortably handled a full shooting day, the dust- and moisture-resistant body shrugged off the elements, and the whole kit rode in my small backpack. Being able to shoot a wide range of subject matter with a single camera and lens was liberating for a hybrid shooter like me. It allowed me to forget about carrying a bag full of heavy lenses and to just focus on being creative. I really enjoyed having a compact and lightweight setup that delivered high-quality images, whether I was shooting at the highest level of professional sports or just enjoying a summer outing with my family. My early impression is that the RX10 V punches well above its weight class and, for me, lands as the most capable do-everything camera Sony has put in a single body to date. If you want to carry less and capture more, this RX10 V belongs on your radar. Are you eyeing the RX10 V as a one-bag travel and sports rig? Share your thoughts in the comments below! Reza is a professional photographer, cinematographer, and educator based in Seattle WA. He specializes in a variety of creative fields, including wedding photography, portrait photography, cinematography, and FAA Part 107 drone aerials. As an educator, Reza's aim is to produce compelling educational content that inspires and empowers creators. I use the Nikon Coolpix1100 as a bridge and for very long reach. It is unmatched in reach. This camera has a huge following and I am sure it will do well. I am not that impressed with the updates outlined. Out of curiosity, what were you expecting with regards to the updates that left you feeling disappointed?

title: Sony RX10 V Review: Sometimes the Best Still Isn’t Good Enough - PetaPixel
content: Sony RX10 V Review: Sometimes the Best Still Isn’t Good Enough Nearly nine years after Sony unveiled the Cyber-shot RX10 IV bridge camera, the company is back with its long-awaited successor, the RX10 V. Much has changed in the photography space since 2017, but unfortunately, I cannot say the same about the RX10 V. The Sony RX10 IV has attracted a huge audience since its 2017 debut. The camera’s winning combination of a reasonably competent stacked 20-megapixel Type 1 sensor, an expansive and versatile 24-600mm-equivalent f/2.4-4 Zeiss lens, and an Alpha-inspired design has made it a go-to bridge camera option for photographers seeking a camera that can just about do it all without fussing with interchangeable lenses. To its credit, the RX10 V offers the same benefits and still fulfills its predecessor’s promise to be good at an impressively wide range of photographic tasks. However, where the Sony RX10 V comes up short is that what perhaps felt impressive nearly a decade ago is not quite so now. Despite a redesigned body and an array of new features, the RX10 V doesn’t feel unquestionably modern. In fact, it feels decidedly old-school in some meaningful ways. It’s not all bad news, of course. There is still a lot to like about the RX10 V. So let’s dive in, see what’s new and analyze what works well, and, more importantly, identify what doesn’t. We’re actually going to get off to a positive start here with the RX10 V, as its redesigned body and overall handling are, by and large, a strong point for Sony’s newest point-and-shoot camera. While the RX10 IV had a perfectly fine design, it was quite old feeling even at the time of its release. In stark contrast, the redesigned RX10 V looks and, even more importantly, feels like a modern Sony Alpha camera. Aside from the large built-in lens and relatively short viewfinder protrusion on the top, the RX10 V looks a lot like a Sony a7-series camera at first glance. It has many of the same controls as well, and those are located in similar spots. For example, one of the biggest improvements here is the introduction of a dedicated autofocus point sub-selector joystick on the back of the camera. It feels and works like the same type of joystick on something like an a7 V. Likewise, AF-ON and Fn buttons are in familiar positions and the camera’s rear directional pad with its rotating dial has dual functions, like pressing left for drive mode and self-timer, right for ISO, and up for your display options. The top of the camera has a very typical mode dial with a secondary rotating control for swapping between photo, video, and S&Q modes. There are a pair of command dials, including one that locks, custom C1 and C2 buttons, and a rocker around the shutter release for controlling zoom. There’s also a rather unusual power switch. It’s not bad, it’s just different than most cameras. Speaking of controlling the lens zoom, I found the rocker switch around the shutter release to be, by far, my preferred way of changing the focal length. While you can change the zoom directly from the lens with a powered zoom ring, it is really slow and requires a lot of rotation. It’s not like the zooming mechanism is that fast when using the rocker switch either, but it’s definitely swifter. What’s definitely a more pleasant thing is the aperture control ring on the lens. While you can certainly control the aperture via the camera body itself if you want, I do like the direct aperture control on the lens, similar to many of Sony’s E-mount lenses. Another big change is the move to a new, larger, higher-res electronic viewfinder. The EVF has gone from a 0.39-type 2.36-million-dot unit with 0.7x magnification to a 0.5-type EVF with 3.69 million dots and 0.78x magnification. It’s a good, sufficiently large, and sharp new EVF, and I’m a big fan. It also has a faster 120 frames per second frame rate and blackout-free shooting, but more on that later. The camera’s other display, the rear three-inch 1.62-million-dot panel, is technically new as well, although it’s not all that different in terms of resolution, increasing from 1.44 million dots. The screen has also moved from a 4:3 aspect ratio to 3:2. Like the RX10 IV, the RX10 V’s screen tilts, but does not swivel. I would have loved to see a fully articulating display here, but that’s a relatively minor quibble. There’s another big change to Sony’s camera system since the RX10 IV hit the scene: a wholesale menu redesign. Fortunately, the RX10 V, like Sony’s other new cameras in the past few years, benefits from this improvement. The UI is essentially like any other Sony camera launched lately, and it’s easy to navigate. Overall, while the redesigned RX10 V has gotten a little bit beefier and a smidge heavier than its predecessor, I really enjoyed carrying it around. It never felt excessive. This is where things start getting significantly more complicated. On paper, there are some changes, but in many fundamental ways, the RX10 V feels a little too familiar and, by extension, outdated. The camera’s 20-megapixel Type 1 stacked Exmor RS CMOS sensor, effectively the same as before, is paired with an upgraded, more powerful Bionz XR processor. This new processor, previously featured in the Sony a7 V late last year and the a7R VI just a couple of months ago, incorporates a dedicated AI processing unit. In theory, this should drive meaningful improvements. In practice, the RX10 V doesn’t actually perform like I expect a modern camera to — at least not in all the areas I was hoping. Let’s get one thing out of the way first: the RX10 V’s image quality is fine. In some situations, it’s even very good. When light is sufficient and ISO can stay low, the RX10 V can deliver some sharp, colorful photos with reasonable enough dynamic range given the sensor’s size. The dynamic range is a far cry from Sony’s APS-C and full-frame cameras, of course, but it’s perfectly serviceable in this product segment. Unfortunately, I was not able to test out the RX10 V’s RAW files due to a lack of beta support in Sony’s Imaging Edge software, but low-ISO JPEGs are entirely satisfactory. The camera will lose shadow and highlight detail faster than any modern interchangeable lens camera on the market, but photographers have accomplished a lot with much worse sensors. I expect that RAW processing will be versatile enough to correct for minor exposure errors and recover some missing detail. Where the problems arise is when the going gets tough, which is something of a pattern with the RX10 V. In low light, the RX10 V struggles. Even at ISO 800, image quality noticeably degrades. At ISO 1600 and 3200, fairly normal ISO settings for most cameras in 2026, the RX10 V has a hard time. I’d love to be able to see what I could do using manual noise reduction on a RAW file, but with JPEG images, the camera’s noise reduction is excessive. Photos get a muddy, overly smooth look. High ISO photos are, frankly, unpleasant to look at. There’s also one more thing worth mentioning. While eventual RAW editing support will solve this issue, the RX10 V’s automatic white balance (AWB) is iffy, at best. In mixed lighting or low-light situations, I found the camera consistently delivered images that were too cool and a bit flat. While recent Sony cameras have improved by leaps and bounds in terms of AWB performance, thanks largely to AI processing improvements, the RX10 V doesn’t really follow suit. The move to the new Bionz XR image processor comes with significant changes to how the RX10 V autofocuses. For example, there is now Real-Time Recognition AF for a wide range of subjects, similar to that of other recent Sony cameras. The RX10 V has 575 autofocus points that cover nearly 71% of the image area. It has all the expected focus-area mode settings, such as four different spot sizes, custom framing, and full-area AF. The biggest improvement here is that Real-Time Recognition AF can recognize and track humans, animals, birds, insects, cars, trains, and planes. There’s also an Auto mode that detects the subject in the frame, though I found it noticeably less reliable when photographing animals than when I manually set the camera to the appropriate subject detection mode. Speaking of unreliability, I admit I expected better autofocus performance from the RX10 V overall. Sometimes the tracking was very good, quickly locking onto a bird or a small mammal. However, when light levels dipped even a little or the background got just the slightest bit busier, the camera could really struggle. At its best, it’s very good. At its worst, though, it’s frustrating. The insect mode was similarly inconsistent. There were times when I was very impressed by the camera’s ability to pick out a bug among a relatively cluttered scene, and then other times when a large insect was front and center, entirely unobscured, and the camera just refused to pick it up. One area where the RX10 V seemingly doesn’t miss a beat at all is when photographing people, for what it’s worth. When the autofocus works, it really works well. It can be quick and decisive. However, I didn’t find it all that reliable, and certainly not up to my standards for today’s camera technology. I think that for people who aren’t necessarily looking to photograph small, fast-moving critters, the RX10 V could prove highly capable. It’s when it is even the least bit challenged that the camera stumbles, and that is, unfortunately, also when I find myself the most frustrated. I know what Sony’s autofocus technology is capable of, and while I likewise know that the RX10 V is not a professional-grade tool, it costs $2,300, which is a serious chunk of change. I think it’s fair to have high expectations, and the RX10 V just doesn’t consistently meet them. On the other hand, the RX10 V’s new Bionz XR processor is mostly good news for continuous shooting performance. The camera can shoot at 30 frames per second, entirely blackout-free, with AF/AE calculations. That’s great. It does come with some caveats, though. This speed requires the electronic shutter, which isn’t surprising. But it also requires shooting lossy RAW files, if you want to shoot RAW at all. That’s a bit more surprising to me, and not ideal when I am trying to have great image quality and speed. On the plus side, the stacked sensor still delivers a usable dynamic range with the electronic shutter. That said, peak dynamic range isn’t particularly great anyway, but it’s nice that, in many ways, there’s not a big penalty for using the electronic shutter. That’s also true for rolling shutter, as it’s not really an issue with this camera thanks to the fast readout speed. There is one pretty glaring omission in the performance department, though. Sony’s other two Bionz XR-equipped cameras have Pre-Capture, which lets you half-press the shutter to record a continuous stream of photos before fully pressing the shutter. This is really useful when photographing unpredictable subjects, like birds or athletes. The RX10 V would really benefit from this feature, and it’s a genuine shame it isn’t here. Like in the RX10 IV, the RX10 V has a mechanical leaf shutter. Leaf shutters are cool and enable flash sync at much faster speeds, but they do come with certain limitations. In the RX10 V’s case, like its predecessor, these limitations are apparent when using certain shutter speed and aperture combinations. When using the camera’s mechanical shutter, any shutter speed faster than 1/1000 second means the aperture stops down to f/8. That’s a very slow aperture for a camera with a relatively small image sensor, ushering in unsightly diffraction that softens images. It’s also a slow aperture in terms of depth of field. The RX10 V can actually deliver really pleasant out-of-focus backgrounds at its maximum aperture, which ranges from f/2.4 at the very widest end to f/4 at 100mm (equivalent). While f/4 may not blow you away, when you’re at equivalent focal lengths like 300-600mm, it can create a nice, soft background in favorable situations. Sometimes the RX10 V’s bokeh punches far above its weight class. But that is not the case at f/8, no matter what you do. So if you want to shoot at 1/2000 or 1/4000 second and f/2.4, f/4, or even f/5.6, you’ll need to use the electronic shutter. And again, while the electronic shutter is good in many ways, it’s not quite as good as mechanical in terms of image quality. The Sony RX10 V is a surprisingly impressive hybrid camera for those seeking an all-in-one, versatile camera. The camera records at 4Kp120 with a slight crop, 4Kp60 at the full width of the image sensor, and supports 4:2:2 10-bit All-I. It also has Sony’s Multi Interface (MI) Shoe, S-Cinetone, S-Log3, LUT support, and slow-motion recording. For those who want to live stream, the RX10 V supports that too at up to 4Kp30. Add in the fact that it has things like Active Mode image stabilization, Auto Framing, (mostly) competent autofocus, and an extremely expansive built-in zoom (plus digital Clear Image Zoom), and there’s an awful lot here to like. While I can safely say the RX10 V did not meet or exceed all of my photographic expectations for a $2,300 bridge camera in 2026, the same cannot be said for its video features and performance. It’s the best in its class by a country mile. In our video review above, Jordan Drake goes into significantly more detail, but the main takeaway here is that it’s a well-rounded video tool with relatively few drawbacks. As Drake says, the RX10 V “beats the pants off” its competitors and is better than any similarly priced camcorders. All the same reasons consumers have tripped over each other trying to grab a Sony RX10 IV for the past eight years still hold true today with the new RX10 V. It remains a very versatile, mostly capable camera that does a pretty good job at just about everything. The tradeoff is that to have a wildly versatile camera like the RX10 V and its 24-600mm f/2.4-4 equivalent lens, the typical photographic experience tops out at “pretty good.” Pretty good image quality, pretty good autofocus, and pretty good operability at a pretty premium price. Sorry, but that doesn’t seem good enough to me. If I had to sum up my experience with the RX10 V, it’s much like when I went hands-on with the RX10 IV back in the day: I constantly feel conflicted. It’s so easy to see the appeal of a bridge camera like the Sony RX10 V. But I must admit, I expected that with eight years of technological advancements and a new processor, the RX10 V could smooth out more of the RX10 IV’s rough edges. I don’t think it does, at least not all of them or to the degree that it should have. Therefore, the RX10 V falls short of its potential. When my subjects were against a blank background in bright light, everything was smooth sailing across the entire zoom range. The RX10 V felt great, and I experienced what makes it a special camera and what made its predecessor one of the most celebrated and popular cameras of its type ever made. But when the real world reared its complex head and the photographic situations became more challenging, the RX10 V felt frustrating instead of fantastic. There were more compromises than I’m comfortable with. For a specific example, I spent a little over an hour camped out on a series of very uncomfortable, slimy rocks on the coast, waiting for some adorable young mink to emerge from their seaweed-covered home. And they did: they played, they ran, and they hunted. It was a really special experience that, on paper, the RX10 V is fully equipped to handle. Instead of excelling, though, it stumbled. Focus was indecisive, forcing me to manually zero in on a small, swift subject. Low-light image quality is poor, meaning that many moments that looked great to my eyes in real life look much less so in photos. My hit rate was not where I expected it to be. There’s no question that I put the RX10 V in a difficult situation, one that I would have fully expected its predecessor to fumble in 2017. But it’s not 2017 anymore, and a prevailing thought I had after it got dark and the mink went back into hiding was, “I wish this camera did a better job.” That’s not what I ever want to think after taking photos of a subject I really enjoy. And then there’s the price of it: $2,300. While that is quite a lot for most photographers, it’s also important to consider: Could I have done better with a $2,300 camera kit comprising an interchangeable lens camera and some sort of telephoto zoom lens? Probably not, no. But I’m not going to give a $2,300 camera a free pass just because it does something unique. That alone is not enough for me to put on blinders. Purely on the value side, the RX10 V’s proposition is attractive. And I believe that for many people, the Sony RX10 V will be an excellent camera that does everything they want and more. I’m just not one of those people. I want more, and I think that is a reasonable demand. If you can find a used Sony RX10 IV, it’s a perfectly viable alternative for users who just want a versatile bridge camera that can do a lot. The RX10 V’s redesigned body is definitely better, as is its much-improved longevity thanks to the switch to a Sony Z-type battery. But I believe some users, especially photographers, would be well served by a cheaper pre-loved RX10 IV. Just don’t expect to pay all that much less for it, though. Maybe the introduction of the Mark V will result in lower Mark IV prices, but at the time of publication, they’re very high. For those who really prioritize zooming and don’t necessarily care a lot about image quality, the Nikon Coolpix P1100 is over $1,000 cheaper than the RX10 V, and it has a 24-3000mm equivalent built-in lens. Yes, that’s right, 3000mm. It has a much smaller 16-megapixel CMOS sensor, the lens stops down to f/8, and the camera itself is plasticky and big. Still, it’s a very reasonable choice for those who care most about documenting wildlife, especially birds. Another compelling choice is the super-affordable Panasonic Lumix FZ80D. It has a small 18-megapixel sensor paired to a 20-1200mm equivalent lens. The image quality is nowhere near as good as that of the Sony RX10 V, but Panasonic’s superzoom is just $450 right now and offers extensive reach. In terms of bridge camera image quality, feature set, and video performance, the Sony RX10 V is the clear winner. It’s really not even close. It just comes down to how much you want to spend and how much you value extreme focal length range. 600mm is a lot, but you can certainly get more if you’re willing to compromise in other areas. I have been wringing my hands over this all-important question. Ultimately, I must cop out a bit here. The answer is “Maybe.” As critical as I have been of the Sony RX10 V and as much as I wish it were better than it is, it’s also the best overall bridge camera, bar none. So if that’s what you want and you are willing to accept the costs, literally and figuratively, the Sony RX10 V is an impressive and attractive option. title: The Sony RX10 V Is the Best Version of My All-Time Favorite Bridge Camera - PCMag
content:
The Sony RX10 V is the best bridge camera ever made, pairing outstanding image quality, class-leading autofocus, and a versatile 24-600mm lens into a rugged all-in-one package that's worth the premium for serious wildlife, sports, and travel photographers. The Sony RX10 V ($2,299.99) is a camera I've wanted Sony to make for years, and it turns out it was worth the wait. The old RX10 IV has been out of production for some time, and the few other bridge superzooms that stuck around couldn't match its picture quality or speed. The RX10 V fills the gap with a large Type 1 image sensor and 24-600mm zoom lens, 30fps continuous drive with bleeding-edge autofocus, a 4K120 video engine, and weather protection for comfortable use outdoors. Yes, it costs more than twice as much as its nearest competitor, the Nikon Coolpix P950 ($849.95), but it's better in every way that counts. The RX10 V is the ultimate all-in-one camera for wildlife, nature, sports, and travel photography, earning an exemplary five-star rating (the first camera in this category to do so since the original RX10) and our Editors' Choice award. Bridge cameras have been around since the days when 35mm film ruled the world, and peaked in popularity in the DSLR era. The concept is pretty straightforward—these cameras use an SLR body style with a fixed lens and a large zoom range. I've never loved the name, but marketing departments would have you believe these cameras bridge the gap between pocket cameras and interchangeable-lens models. They've also been called superzooms, megazooms, or even ultrazooms, though those definitions got a little muddy as pocket cameras got longer and longer zoom ranges. For instance, the Lumix ZS99's 30x lens is just as worthy of the superzoom moniker. Quibbles about the category name aside, the RX10 V ticks all the boxes for a bridge camera. From a distance, it looks like a mirrorless camera with a mid-sized zoom attached, and its body and controls make it handle very much like an interchangeable lens model like the Sony a7 V. The lens doesn't come off, but it covers an incredible range. In full-frame terms, its angle of view is 24-600mm, and its F2.4-4.0 aperture means that its Type 1 sensor can capture good-looking photos in tough light. The benefits for photographers who like to capture subjects that require a big, heavy zoom, like the Sigma 150-600mm F5-6.3 DG DN OS Sports (10.5 by 4.3 inches, 4.6 pounds) for mirrorless cams, are obvious. The RX10 V offers the same angle of view when zoomed in, captures wider scenes, and is far easier to carry—it measures 3.7 by 5.4 by 5.2 inches (HWD) and weighs 2.5 pounds. You're losing something in image quality, since general-purpose full-frame cameras offer more pixels (33MP for the Sony a7 V and Canon EOS R6 Mark III, versus the RX10 V's 20MP) and deliver more detail at higher ISOs, more than making up for the RX10 V's brighter optics. But if you don't want to carry a big kit or suffer from arthritis or another condition that makes heavy telezooms unwieldy, bridge cameras can help you get out and enjoy nature and wildlife photography. Bridge cameras aren't as numerous as they once were, and there are so few on the market that I questioned if the category would survive. The RX10 V stands apart as the only one with a Type 1 image sensor. The Panasonic FZ80D, the Nikon P950, and the Nikon P1100 all use Type 1/2.3 chips, a sensor format that's about a quarter the size of the RX10 V's chip and shows correspondingly less detail and additional noise in tough light. There is one area where smaller sensors win, though—the P950 and P1100 have significantly longer lenses, reaching 2,000mm and 3,000mm respectively. I think that's overkill for most subjects, even for small, camera-shy songbirds, but there's no question they magnify far-off subjects better, with the caveat that atmospheric haze in hot, humid weather will absolutely show up in images at those focal lengths. Still, the RX10 V's 600mm zoom matches the angle of view of the lenses I typically use for birding with a full-frame camera, and because its sensor is larger than those in other bridge cams, its photos can handle a bit of cropping too. To me, the benefits of the big sensor and the RX10 V's impressive focus system (more on that later) outweigh the shorter overall reach, though I wouldn't say "no" to an RX10 VI with a lens that reached an 800mm angle of view. The P950 ($849.95) and P1100 ($1,149.95) are also less expensive. At around $2,300, the RX10 V costs more than any other bridge camera ever. Inflation plays a role: The RX10 IV cost around $1,700 when it debuted in 2017, and the RX10 V's price just about matches the inflation rate. The RX10 IV was an expensive camera when it came out, too, but I'm sure Sony is comfortable pricing the RX10 V north of $2,000 given its upgraded features, and used copies of the RX10 IV are selling in the $2,000 to $3,000 range in recent weeks. I'm sure RX10 IV prices will drop now that the RX10 V is available, but demand for this type of camera means photographers are willing to pay a lot for one. Nature and travel photography are two disciplines where a bridge camera makes sense. When you're out in the wild photographing animals, you'll often want to switch to a wide lens for a landscape scene, or a macro lens to capture an interesting bit of texture or an insect. The RX10 V does all that with one lens and supports worry-free outdoor use. It includes seals around buttons and in the lens that reduce the risk of dust or water getting inside, so you can use it comfortably in nature, even when the storm clouds roll in. Sony doesn't go as far as to test it to IP standards, but you should feel comfortable using it in rainy weather. Just remember that weather-sealed doesn't mean waterproof; the camera isn't submersible like an action cam. The weather protection comes at the cost of one feature: The built-in flash from previous models in the line is gone from the RX10 V. I don't see that as a huge drawback; a small pop-up flash doesn't have the reach to light up distant subjects, and can create a shadow on nearer ones because of the length of the lens. You can add an external flash if you want the option to snap some backlit portraits. The RX10 V has a hot shoe, and the tiny Godox iT30Pro is a perfect fit for the camera—it's small enough to keep in your pocket, doesn't cost much, and includes automatic TTL power control. I tested the Godox flash previously with the Canon PowerShot V1 and walked away happy. The body feels sturdy, too. There's a little more plastic on the exterior versus an a7 V, but it's a high-grade material, not the cheap-feeling flimsy type, and there are a few metal bits that add some class. A textured leatherette covers the grip and much of the body, helping you keep a firm grip on the camera. And speaking of the grip, it's great. It curves gently, making the camera comfortable to use one-handed, with a middle-finger indentation and an angled shutter release that falls right under my index finger. Creators with larger hands may find it a little small; I wear medium-sized gloves and find my pinky finger hanging partway off the bottom, but I don't have any problems wielding the camera one-handed, and there's about an eighth of an inch of clearance between the tops of my fingers and the lens, so I didn't run into problems with my knuckles scraping up against the barrel. Sony tells me that the RX10 V uses the same "design language" as its full-frame a7 line, and I'm not about to disagree. Its control scheme, menus, and overall interface aren't much different from those of the company's interchangeable-lens cameras. I'm happy for the consistency. It makes the RX10 V a good fit for pros and hobbyists who also use a Sony a7 camera, and the basic controls are familiar to anyone who knows their way around a camera. Beginners may be intimidated, but the RX10 V is tuned to get good results in automatic mode, and is even better with a few tweaks to settings and button functions. Controls start on the top plate. The shutter release is in its expected location, sitting atop the handgrip at a slight angle. It's surrounded by a Wide/Tight rocker that adjusts the zoom. The C1 and C2 buttons are just behind, and both are configurable; by default, C1 maps to White Balance, and C2 changes the autofocus mode. I typically use auto white balance with this type of camera, so I set C1 to cycle through the autofocus subject-detection modes I use most often—humans, animals, birds, and insects. I left C2 as-is, as having quick access to change the area of interest for the autofocus system is beneficial. I go into more detail on the autofocus system and which settings to use in different scenarios further down the page. The On/Off switch, shutter speed dial, exposure value (EV) compensation dials, and a nested pair of Mode dials round out the top controls. EV brightens or darkens the exposure with a twist, with the results immediately visible in the viewfinder, and includes a push-button toggle lock so you don't jostle it by accident. The top Mode dial controls the exposure setting, and the bottom switches between stills, movies, and slow and quick-motion (S&Q) video. For exposure modes, the RX10 V includes a full Auto option, plus Program (like Auto, but with support for EV adjustment), Aperture, Shutter, and full Manual, plus two custom modes (1, 2) that you can configure to taste, and a star (*) option that stores up to an additional ten custom modes. That's probably overkill, but custom modes can come in handy—for example, you could set up options to quickly change between a long exposure for landscapes and a short one for action. The Menu button is on the rear, all the way over at the top left corner, out of the way so you aren't likely to tap it while you're trying to take a picture. The buttons you'll use during capture are all on the right half. Record (to start and stop movies) is next to the viewfinder eyecup, and AF-ON is just to its right. A joystick to move the active focus point is just below, along with an Fn button that opens an on-screen menu, a flat dial with four directional presses, and a center enter/confirm button, Play, and Delete/C3 finish it off. With the exception of Menu, all of the rear controls are configurable. The C3 button toggles the touch screen by default, and the flat dial's directional presses set Display (up), ISO (right), and Drive/Self-Timer (left) out of the box. But if any of these aren't useful, you can dive into the menu system and change it up—there are literally dozens of assignable functions, and nearly every option in the menu is available. The lens includes three discrete control rings for aperture, zoom, and manual focus, along with a function button (Focus Hold by default), an AF/MF toggle, an autofocus distance limiter with settings for distant targets only (3 meters to infinity) or Full to cover close-ups and macros too, and a toggle switch to change the aperture ring between clicked f-stops or smooth, continuous adjustment. Likewise, the on-lens zoom control has three settings—Standard, Quick, or Step—and the latter switches between prime focal lengths with each twist (24, 28, 35, 50, 70, 85, 100, 135, 200, 300, 400, 500, and 600mm). I find the default layout pretty good overall, but I made a few additional tweaks. I changed the Drive/Self-Timer button to a toggle to cycle through the options I use most often (Single, Hi/15fps, and Mid/10fps), set the OK button to engage the Speed Boost (which ramps the drive speed up to the fastest 30fps), and since I'm not a back button focus person and kept hitting AF-ON instead of Record when trying to start a movie, I set both to Record. You get the idea—if you want to make a button to do something that the camera can do, you probably can. What's more, you can set up separate customizations for stills and movies if you want. The RX10 V includes an on-screen Fn menu and a full multi-page text menu. Fn puts commonly used functions at the surface. It includes 12 options that are configurable (as you may have guessed), with a default set that includes JPG color mode, metering, file format, focus, stabilization, and shutter options. The full menu includes a main screen with another batch of quick-access options, a configurable My Menu page, and a lengthy set of options (another 55 pages' worth). Camera experts will find all of this pretty familiar, but the sheer breadth of options and depth of the menus are going to intimidate folks stepping up from a more basic bridge camera or even a smartphone. My best advice is to use the camera for a bit to figure out which options you're diving into the menus to change, and then take the time to configure the buttons and menus to your taste. I've shared some of my preferred tweaks here, and Sony's searchable online manual is a great resource too. The RX10 V features two displays: a tilting touch LCD on the rear and an eye-level viewfinder. The LCD is a typical Sony: a 3-inch panel with a 1.62-million-dot resolution and touch support, mounted on a single-axis hinge that supports upward and downward tilt. It's absolutely adequate compared with displays on interchangeable-lens cameras and is far better than the 921k, non-touch displays that Nikon uses for the P950 and P1100. The RX10 V's LCD is hard to see in bright light at default settings, but it includes a Sunny Weather mode that boosts its backlight for better visibility. Annoyingly, the Monitor Brightness/Sunny Weather setting is not assignable to a Fn menu button, but you can put it on the My Menu page, which I recommend, as it's an option you'll likely use frequently. The EVF is a stunner for the class. It's as large as the viewfinders in premium full-frame cameras (0.78x magnification), sharp enough that you'll have no problem gauging focus and exposure (3.68 million dots), and shows smooth motion with a selectable 60/120fps refresh rate. The 120fps mode isn't quite as sharp as the default 60fps rate, but it is worth using if you're photographing sports or other scenes where you want to pan the camera to follow a moving subject. Earlier models in the RX10 series used Sony's NP-FW50 battery, a rechargeable that's underpowered by modern standards and has mostly fallen out of use since the RX10 IV's release. It's been replaced here by the NP-FZ100, which is considered one of the best rechargeables from any brand. It's a good move; the RX10 V is rated for a healthy 570 EVF/630 LCD exposures per charge under CIPA standards, and you'll get more than that in burst mode. It's enough to get you through most days of photography. It's worthwhile to check that you have power-saving settings enabled in the menu, as my review sample shipped with them disabled. I suspect that's because of the extended zoom. When the camera goes to sleep, the lens retracts, and waking it back up takes a beat, plus the lens itself requires about 2.4 seconds to zoom from 24mm to 600mm. For birding, I'm almost always at 600mm, so I set an aggressive (10 seconds) timeout for the LCD and EVF (Monitor Off), and a longer Power Save Start Time (sleep) length (5 minutes). One note: You must have the sleep option enabled for the Monitor Off power saving option to work. I didn't realize this during my first photo walk with the camera and burned through about 60% of the battery over three hours in the woods chasing songbirds because the camera never went to sleep. The camera includes a hot shoe for an external flash (none is built in) and supports sync with its mechanical shutter at 1/1,000-second at wider apertures (F2.4-7.1) and 1/2,000-second at stopped-down apertures (F8-16). It has a pair of USB connections, one USB-C for charging, data transfer, and UVC/UAC live streaming, a legacy micro USB 2.0 port that works with remote shutter release and intervalometers like the ShutterBoss (the camera also has a built-in intervalometer for time lapses), micro HDMI, and discrete 3.5mm microphone and headphone jacks. There is a single memory card slot supporting UHS-II SDXC memory cards. Most recording modes work with cards with a V30 speed rating, but you will need a V60 or faster for the highest-quality (280Mbps) 4K120. For more details on SD card speed ratings, check out our explainer. I tested the camera with a V90/299MBps Sony Tough card. A fast card is handy for burst capture. I managed 175 Compressed Raw images at 30fps before the capture rate started to slow down, and noted a 12-second time to clear a full buffer to the card. For JPGs, I got 265 images with a 7-second clear time. The RX10 V's electronic shutter only works with JPGs and Compressed Raw. You can switch to Lossless Compressed and use the mechanical shutter for 10fps bursts, a pace it maintains for about 235 exposures with an 8-second buffer clear. The RX10 V works with a smartphone app, the Sony Creators' App, available for Android and Apple devices. The camera connects to phones or tablets using a mix of Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and the app supports file transfers, remote control, and firmware updates. The RX10 V prompts you to connect to your smartphone during the initial setup process, though it's not a requirement—the camera works fine without the app and does not require activation. The RX10 IV had, for its day, the best autofocus you could get in a bridge camera. The RX10 V earns the same accolades, but I can't stress enough how much it's improved over the Mark IV. The RX10 V uses the same focus-tracking system and subject-recognition features as Sony's latest full-frame cameras, including the a7 V and a7R VI, which are far more advanced and intelligent than the system in the RX10 IV. It adds Real Time Tracking, a feature that identifies a subject and stays with it as it moves through the frame, as well as smart subject detection for humans, animals, birds, insects, cars and trains, airplanes, and includes a combined animal and bird option, as well as an auto mode that can detect any of these subject types. Subject detection works very well. It jumps to the eyes of a person, animal, bird, or insect, taking some of the work of setting the focus point off of your shoulders. There are numerous areas of interest to start focus, too. It includes several sizes of flexible spots (a box that you can move around), an expanded spot (my favorite for birds in brush and branches; it looks at the center first and then the surrounding areas), several larger zones, and a wide setting that looks at nearly the entirety of the image sensor to set focus. The latter is great for pets and kids at play, letting you focus on catching a moment without worrying about where the focus target is. The autofocus system covers about 70% of the image sensor, leaving only the outer edges untouched. I used the RX10 V for pet snaps and birding at a wooded trail and am wowed by how well the focus system performs. It reliably finds its target in most situations and is fast. I got snaps of catbirds chomping on bugs, a hyperactive American redstart bouncing through branches, and other subjects that other bridge cameras would fail to catch in focus. To compare, I tested the Nikon P1100 at the same trail and in similar light, and walked away frustrated. The P1100's contrast-detection autofocus struggled to lock onto birds perched on branches; its system is sloth-like compared with the RX10 V. I won't go as far as to call the Sony perfect, though. I ran into a few instances where it struggled. I caught a catbird in relatively dim light, sitting on a branch with no foreground obstructions, but the camera was slow to reach the right starting point. The scene had very little contrast, just a gray bird and a lot of leaves, all in shadow, and the lens was way out of focus to start. The bird was pretty close, and my previous images had been at a long distance. I was able to get the focus right by targeting a nearby tree trunk and then moving the camera back to the bird, but by then it had retreated further into the tree. On the other hand, I got photos with the RX10 V that I'd never dream of getting with another bridge camera. I had several opportunities to use its insect-focus mode and 1:2 life-size macro focus capability to capture stunning images of dragonflies and damselflies, both posed on objects and in flight. Sure, the RX10 V can struggle with scenes that combine dim light and low contrast, but that's true of any camera, even a big full-frame mirrorless. The 30fps maximum capture rate is impressive, though it's a bit much for many situations. I stuck with a 15fps burst rate for the most part and found it more than sufficient. Still, there are times when 30fps comes in handy. The RX10 V supports a Speed Boost feature that lets you switch the drive mode to 30fps with a single button press. It's not mapped by default and can be assigned as either a press-and-hold or a toggle button. The high speed makes the RX10 V a viable option for action photography. It has a couple of drawbacks versus a full-frame mirrorless, though. One is the electronic zoom lens. The 24-600mm is pretty zippy (it goes from its widest to its tightest angle in about 2.4 seconds), but that's still enough lag to miss a shot if you're photographing field sports or other scenes where you'll want to frequently change the focal length. The camera is also missing precapture, a mode that continuously buffers images to temporary memory as the camera focuses, letting you save the buffer (usually about a half-second) and then write images going forward to memory. During my tech briefing on the RX10 V's features a representative from Sony US said that it made a request to add precapture with the engineers in Japan, which I see as a strong hint that it will be rolled out in a firmware update, though I won't go as far as to call it a guarantee. The RX10 V's 24-600mm F2.4-4.0 and 20MP Type 1 Stacked CMOS image sensor are a cut above the other bridge cameras available today—the Nikon P950, P1100, and Lumix FZ80D all use far smaller Type 1/2.3 chips and lenses that gather less light. A larger sensor and more light generally result in better image quality, so the RX10 V has an inherent advantage. Details are stronger overall, and you've got some room to crop without losing a decent photo. For instance, I cropped an image of an indigo bunting to 2MP, and it's a perfect shot to share on a birding site to log a sighting, as the species is identifiable and the details are good enough for that purpose. I'd stick to more modest crops for images you plan to print, but you can knock it down to 10MP (840mm equivalent) or 5MP (1,200mm equivalent) and still get an image that will pop on social media, making the lens a little more versatile for distant subjects. The image sensor supports an ISO range of 64-12800 in either JPG or Raw format. I've not yet had a chance to look at Raw images in our standard processor, as Lightroom Classic has not yet been updated to read files from the RX10 V. That said, its JPGs are right in line with what I've seen from the Type 1 Exmor RS sensor when used in other cameras with newer Sony processors, like the ZV-1 Mark II. Photos show excellent detail and very little visible noise from ISO 100-1600. Fine lines show signs of smudging around the edges and start to blur together at ISO 3200, and pretty much disappear at ISO 6400. Noise adds a rough veil of texture at ISO 12800. I'll hold off on Raw analysis until Adobe rolls out its next regularly scheduled Lightroom update. But based on my experience with other cameras using the sensor, a Raw format will better preserve detail at ISO 3200-6400, albeit with some added texture from luminance noise, and give you the leeway to edit and tone the exposure, colors, and white balance to taste. As with any sensor, you'll have the most room to edit without harming picture quality at lower ISOs. If you don't want to fuss with Raw capture, Sony includes several stylized looks for JPG modes. The RX10 V includes the typical selection from other recent cameras like the a7R VI: Black and White, Film, Film 2, Film 3, Instant, Neural, Portrait, Sepia, Soft Highkey, Standard, Vivid, and Vivid 2. I used Film 3 for a lot of my images for this review; it's a nice look with saturated colors and lifted black levels, a good choice for wildlife scenes in mixed lighting. I also played with the Dynamic Range Optimization (DRO) option for some scenes. DRO has been around forever, but received an upgrade with the latest image processor, adding three new levels, DRO 6-8, that deliver a near-HDR look to scenes. You've got to select these settings manually (there's an Auto DRO setting that selects from DRO 1-5), but I found DRO 6 was ideal to get the tone I wanted for the long exposure image of water flowing out of a pavilion (above)—the Auto option left the shadows a little too crunched for my taste. I think DRO 7 and 8 are a little too extreme for most scenes—they look a little fake, but if you run into a shot with very dark shadows and bright highlights, you may want to push DRO to its limit. DRO is for JPGs; if you use a Raw format, you can get a similar look by moving Lightroom's Shadows and Black Level sliders to the right. The lens is stellar. It dates back to the RX10 III, and delivers sharp, detailed results through its entire range. I ran a fresh round of SFRPlus resolution tests in Imatest and the results are right in line with what I expect from previous iterations. The camera delivers its clearest, highest-contrast photos at f/2.4-8, with outstanding results for a 20MP sensor, recording between 2,500 and 2,900 lines. Importantly, the lens delivers clear results across the entire frame at most focal lengths, except at 24mm. At 24mm f/2.4, the edges are a little soft, which is pretty common for a superzoom's wildest angle and aperture. Thankfully, the edges sharpen up nicely from f/4 to f/8, the sweet spot for landscape scenes. The lens also supports narrow apertures. You can ratchet the f-stop down to f/16, though I recommend avoiding doing so. Optical diffraction, a physical effect that causes light particles to scatter as they pass through a small opening, sets in starting at f/11 and noticeably softens details. Because of this, it's wise to use a 72mm neutral density filter to cut incoming light if you want to use the camera for long exposures during daylight hours. It's a shame Sony didn't manage to fit an in-lens ND filter, especially since the original RX10 and RX10 II had one, as it's a useful feature for long-exposure landscape photography and video too. There is an upside to diffraction—the scattered light particles render tiny particles of light as diffraction spikes, usually called sunstars. The RX10 V's lens can create the effect, though, as you can see in this example captured at 24mm f/16, the tines aren't well-defined, and there's some visible ghosting (a type of lens flare created by internal reflections). I ran into some instances with flare when making images with the sun just outside of frame at wide apertures, though nothing that surprised me. The preceding image, a wooden bridge nearly entirely in shadow with the sun peeking through the trees and positioned right at the edge of the frame, is a worst-case scenario. And despite the strong backlight and colorful ghost, the image maintains contrast and detail quite well—you can typically avoid visible flare with a slight shift in angle in backlit scenes. The catbird in the following photo was in shadow with the sun behind the trees, for example. The RX10 V can get some bokeh, too. Its long focal length, oversized sensor (for a compact), and relatively wide aperture combine to create background blur, most noticeable when there is some distance between the subject and the background, or when working at macro distances. Backgrounds often melt into nothing, but you'll likely notice some false texture in bright defocused highlights, and the lens can draw some false purple and green color just off the plane of focus—you can see both in the image of the spiderweb below. This combination gives backgrounds a characterful look, and to be fair, even high-end zooms like the Sony FE 200-600mm F5.6-6.3 G OSS can draw scenes with visible texture in specular highlights. An ND filter is also a smart accessory for shutterbugs who want to use the lens wide open in daylight at the highest quality Lossless Compressed Raw format, or with flash, as both are only available with the mechanical shutter. This in-lens leaf shutter supports a minimum 1/1,000-second speed at f/2.4-7.1 and a 1/2,000-second rate at f/8-16, settings that can lead to overexposed images in bright conditions, even at the lowest ISO 100 sensitivity setting. Of course, this isn't at all a concern for taking JPG photos without an add-on flash, or using the camera's Compressed Raw capture mode. The camera uses a fully electronic shutter with a minimum exposure time of 1/16,000 second, so you'll rarely, if ever, have a problem using the lens at f/2.4 in bright daylight with the e-shutter. The RX10 V isn't just a versatile stills camera; it's a standout for video, too. It records high-quality 10-bit 4:2:2 4K video at 24fps or 60fps using the full sensor width, plus it has a crop mode that pushes 4K120 for epic slow-motion footage. The crop is noticeable; it's about 1.5x to my eye, which is a downer for wide landscape shots where you want to slow down running water, or for cityscapes where you want to slow traffic and pedestrians, but a benefit for wildlife and macro scenes, as it gets a closer view of the subject. It's a little odd that Sony doesn't include 4K30, but it's not a big problem in most scenarios, as you can always record at 4K60 and edit the footage on a 4K30 timeline. The exception is low-light, so you'll want to drop down to 4K24 for concerts or video shot in typical home interior lighting. You can select from any of the still profiles for movies, or opt for S-Cinetone, a profile that lives up to its name and captures a Hollywood-style color grade without editing. Experts can switch to S-Log3 for a flat, neutral starting point that supports creative color correction and performs well in high-contrast scenes with both bright highlights and dark shadows. The lens includes optical stabilization, which does a good job at wider focal lengths, and works in conjunction with Digital Active Stabilization, which crops into the frame but nets steadier handheld footage at telephoto focal lengths and macro focus distances. The video looks great, and I think the 4K120 mode is one of the best upgrades versus the RX10 IV. Yes, you can record 1080p slow-motion at higher frame rates with the Mark IV (240, 480, or 960fps), but it's a real pain. You have to use an HFR mode on the RX10 IV, which records a short 4-second clip and then slows it down in-camera in real time, from 30 seconds to 2 minutes, depending on the frame rate. The 240fps mode looks pretty good, but picture quality falls off a cliff at higher frame rates. With the RX10 V, you can record 4K120 in-camera with sound, so you can drop it onto a 30 or 60fps timeline to run at normal speed, or use your video editing software to slow it down. If you want slow motion without editing, switch to S&Q mode, and you'll get footage already slowed, sans audio, with no long wait for in-camera processing. I used the RX10 V's internal microphone during my review. It's a typical built-in mic, with omnidirectional pickup that hears everything around the camera and tends to get overwhelmed in noisy environments. External mics are an option, though; the camera has a 3.5mm mic input jack and works with Sony's line of digital microphones via its hot shoe, so you can upgrade the audio if you want. I'm not being hyperbolic when I say that the Sony RX10 V is the best bridge camera ever made. Its 24-600mm zoom lens can handle nearly any scene, its Type 1 sensor rivals the best smartphones for picture quality, and its autofocus system is right up there with what pros are used to from the latest mirrorless cameras. Weather-sealed construction, 4K120 video, and a very reasonable carry weight seal the deal. Nikon is still the champ when it comes to absolute zoom power, but its P950 and P1100 are huge and slow in comparison, with lesser image quality. Simply put, there's no other fixed-lens camera on sale today that comes close. The RX10 V is peerless in performance and utility, and serves as the benchmark for all other bridge cameras to beat, earning it a rare five-star rating and Editors' Choice honors. Yes. The RX10 V may use the same lens and sensor as the RX10 IV, but everything else gets a major update. It has far better autofocus, improved video and slow motion, a longer-lasting battery, a larger viewfinder, and better construction with protection against dust and splashes, making it worth the upgrade. Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 14 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones. title: The Sony RX10 V Upgrades the Bridge Camera Experience for $2,299 - PetaPixel
content: The Sony RX10 V Upgrades the Bridge Camera Experience for $2,299 When the Sony RX10 IV arrived on the scene in 2017, bringing with it a new stacked Type 1 20-megapixel sensor and a Zeiss-engineered 24-600mm f/2.4-4 equivalent Vario-Sonnar T* built-in lens, it quickly attracted fanfare. It was undoubtedly the best bridge camera on the market as soon as it arrived. Nearly eight years later, its successor, the RX10 V, brings these familiar features alongside some requested updates and looks poised to help Sony keep its crown. What isn’t meaningfully different on the RX10 V are the image sensor and lens. This core imaging pipeline is the same. Sony is still using its 20.1-megapixel stacked Type 1 Exmor RS CMOS image sensor and the Zeiss Vario-Sonnar 24-600mm f/2.4-4 equivalent lens (actual focal length is 9.1-210mm). Beyond that, though, nearly everything is upgraded. The RX10 V features a redesigned camera body that is much closer to its Alpha-series peers, including a very familiar shape, Sony’s latest menu design, a dedicated autofocus sub-selector joystick, and an unmistakably Alpha-esque control layout. There’s a new, larger, sharper EVF that is up from a 0.39-type 2.36M dot EVF with 0.7x magnification to a 0.5-type 3.69M dot panel with 0.78x magnification. There’s a new screen with more pixels, but it’s still a 3-inch panel that only tilts up and down. Further, Sony has moved from its archaic NP-FW50 battery used in the RX10 IV to the much more modern NP-FZ100 battery, which delivers more than a 50% improvement in longevity. The redesigned body is ever-so-slightly larger than the RX10, increasing by 0.5 to 6.3 millimeters across its width, height, and thickness. It’s a negligible increase in overall volume, joined by an even smaller uptick in weight from 1,095 grams (38.6 ounces) to 1,111 grams (39.2 ounces) when the battery and a single UHS-II SD card are inserted. The new body also has better dust and moisture resistance, per Sony. With the benefit of technological advancement, Sony has also moved from Micro USB to USB-C, added 5 GHz Wi-Fi, and included its Multi Interface (MI) Shoe on top. The RX10 V incorporates Sony’s Bionz XR processor, first seen in last year’s a7 V and, more recently, the a7R VI. This new processor has an integrated AI processing unit, which drives improved Real-time Recognition AF with subject detection for people, animals, and numerous types of vehicles. There’s also now Real-time Tracking, allowing the user to select the subject they want to track using the camera’s touchscreen. Continuous maximum shooting speed has increased slightly from 24 fps to 30 fps, and the 30 fps shooting mode is fully blackout-free. There is still no Pre-Capture shooting here on the RX10 V, though. There are significant improvements in video performance. The RX10 IV topped out at 4Kp30 recording in XAVC S/ACVHD. The new RX10 V ups the ante, offering 4Kp60 full width recording and 4Kp120 with a slight crop. The camera has 4:2:2 10-bit All-I recording, plus XAVC HS and XVC S-I. It can also do S&Q recording, something its predecessor lacked. The RX10 V can do live streaming at 4Kp30, whereas the RX10 IV didn’t offer any streaming functionality at all. Additional new video features and functions include Active Mode image stabilization, Auto Framing, S-Cinetone, S-Log3, user LUT support, and a vertical user interface. The Sony RX10 V is available for preorder now for $2,299 in the United States and $2,899 in Canada. Sony says it will begin arriving to customers around August 6. It is worth noting that while the RX10 V arrives with a significantly higher price than its 2017 predecessor, which launched for $1,700, Sony no longer makes the RX10 IV. The now-outdated RX10 IV remains in very high demand and used versions of the camera sell for as much as $3,000 in good condition.
